modern:
Israel’s long, tiring years of wandering were over, and they had finally reached the rest God promised them. No more packing up tents, no more poisonous snakes, no more fierce Amalekite raiders, no more howling wilderness. They had come to the land flowing with milk and honey, and they ate the grain that grew there.

Dear Christian reader, this year the same may happen to you or to me. That’s a joyful thing to look forward to, and if our faith is active and alive, the thought will bring us pure delight. To be with Jesus in the rest God has kept for his people is a wonderful hope, and to think it might come this soon doubles the joy. Unbelief shudders at the river Jordan, which still runs between us and that good land. But we can be sure of this: we’ve already been through more trouble than death at its very worst can do to us. So let’s put every fearful thought away and be glad, really glad, that this may be the year we begin to be “for ever with the Lord.”

Some of God’s people will stay on earth this year to go on serving their Lord. If that’s where we find ourselves, the New Year’s text can still be true for us. “We who have believed do enter into rest.” The Holy Spirit is the down payment on everything we’re going to inherit. He gives us “glory begun below.”

The people in heaven are safe, and so are we, kept safe in Christ Jesus. They’ve won the victory over their enemies, and we win victories too. They enjoy close fellowship with their Lord, and that isn’t kept from us either. They rest in his love, and we have perfect peace in him. They sing his praise, and we get to bless him too. This year we’ll gather the fruit of heaven on earthly ground, where faith and hope have turned the desert into the garden of the Lord. Long ago people ate angels’ food in the wilderness, so why not us, now? Oh, for the grace to feed on Jesus, and so to eat the fruit of the land of Canaan this year!

notes.note: Two dangers of Israel’s wilderness years: poisonous snakes ([[Num.21.6|Numbers 21:6]]) and a desert tribe that attacked them on the way out of Egypt ([[Exod.17.8|Exodus 17:8]]).
In older English, grain of any kind, here wheat or barley, not the corn on the cob we know.
Pure, with nothing mixed in, like a metal that hasn’t been blended with a cheaper one.
From [[Heb.4.9|Hebrews 4:9]], “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.” “Remaineth” means it is still waiting for us.
Israel crossed the river Jordan to enter Canaan. Christians of Spurgeon’s day used it as a picture of death, the last river to cross before heaven.
The opening line of a well-loved hymn by James Montgomery, taken from [[1Thess.4.17|1 Thessalonians 4:17]], “so shall we ever be with the Lord.”
A great army or crowd; here, all of God’s people.
A deposit paid up front to promise the rest will follow. Paul calls the Holy Spirit “the earnest of our inheritance” ([[Eph.1.14|Ephesians 1:14]]).

From Isaac Watts’s hymn “Come, We That Love the Lord”: “The men of grace have found / Glory begun below.” The next lines, “Celestial fruits on earthly ground / From faith and hope may grow,” are the ones Spurgeon borrows a few sentences later.
The manna God fed Israel with in the wilderness. [[Ps.78.25|Psalm 78:25]] says, “Man did eat angels’ food.”

modern:
“We will be glad and rejoice in thee.” We won’t open the gates of this new year to the gloomy notes of a mourning horn. We’ll open them to the sweet music of the harp of joy and the loud, ringing cymbals of gladness. “O come, let us sing unto the Lord: let us make a joyful noise unto the rock of our salvation.” We, the called and faithful and chosen, will drive our griefs away and raise our banners of confidence in the name of God. Others can grieve over their troubles. We have the tree that turns Marah’s bitter pool sweet, and we’ll praise the Lord with joy. Eternal Spirit, our Comforter whose comfort never fails, we are the temples you live in, and we’ll never stop worshiping and blessing the name of Jesus.

*We will*: we’ve made up our minds about it. Jesus must have the crown of our heart’s delight. We won’t dishonor our Bridegroom by mourning while he’s with us. We’ve been appointed to be the musicians of heaven, so let’s rehearse our everlasting song now, before we sing it in the halls of the New Jerusalem.

*We will be glad and rejoice*: two words with one meaning, double joy, blessing on top of blessing. Does our joy in the Lord need any limit, even now? Don’t people who know his grace find their Lord as fragrant as henna and nard, sweet cane and cinnamon, even here? What better perfume will they have in heaven itself?

*We will be glad and rejoice in thee*. That last word is the meat in the dish, the kernel inside the nut, the heart of the whole verse. What heavens are stored up in Jesus! What rivers of endless joy have their source in him, yes, and every drop of their fullness too! Sweet Lord Jesus, you are your people’s portion right now. Give us such a sense of how precious you are this year that from its first day to its last we may be glad and rejoice in you. Let January open with joy in the Lord, and let December close with gladness in Jesus.

notes.note: Sorrowful, mournful.
An early trombone. The King James Bible names it in [[Dan.3.5|Daniel 3:5]]. Spurgeon sets its low, sad notes against the bright harp and cymbals.

At Marah the water was too bitter to drink, until God showed Moses a tree to throw in and the water turned sweet ([[Exod.15.23-Exod.15.25|Exodus 15:23–25]]). Christians have long read the tree as a picture of the cross.
Effective; actually doing what it sets out to do.
Jesus said his friends couldn’t fast and mourn while the bridegroom was with them ([[Mark.2.19|Mark 2:19]]).

notes.term: Camphire and spikenard, calamus and cinnamon
notes.note: Spices from [[Song.4.13-Song.4.14|Song of Solomon 4:13–14]]. Camphire is henna, spikenard (nard) a costly perfumed oil, calamus a sweet-smelling cane.
Yes, indeed.
A share of an inheritance. When God is “our portion,” he himself is what we inherit, and he is enough ([[Ps.73.26|Psalm 73:26]]).

modern:
It’s striking how much of the Bible is about prayer, whether it’s giving us examples, laying down commands or making promises. We’ve hardly opened the Bible before we read, “Then began men to call upon the name of the Lord;” and just as we’re about to close it, we hear the “Amen” of an earnest prayer. The examples are everywhere. Here’s Jacob wrestling, there’s Daniel praying three times a day, and here’s David calling on his God with all his heart. On the mountain we see Elijah; in the prison, Paul and Silas. We have countless commands to pray and endless promises for those who do.

What does all this teach us, if not that prayer is sacred, important and necessary? We can be sure that whatever God made prominent in his Word, he meant to stand out in our lives too. If he said a lot about prayer, it’s because he knows we need it a lot. Our needs run so deep that we must not stop praying until we’re in heaven.

Do you feel you need nothing? Then I’m afraid you don’t know how poor you really are. Is there no mercy you need to ask God for? Then may the Lord in his mercy show you how miserable you are! A soul without prayer is a soul without Christ. Prayer is the first babbling words of a newborn believer, the battle cry of a believer in the fight, the last song of a dying saint falling asleep in Jesus. It’s a Christian’s breath, watchword, comfort, strength and honor.

If you’re a child of God, you’ll seek your Father’s face and live in your Father’s love. Pray that this year you’ll be holy, humble, eager and patient. Pray for closer fellowship with Christ, and that you’ll come more often into the banquet hall of his love. Pray that you’ll be an example and a blessing to others, and that you’ll live more for your Master’s glory. Our motto for this year must be, “Continue in prayer.”

notes.note: The Bible. “Writ” is an old word for something written.

notes.term: “Then began men to call upon the name of the Lord”
notes.note: From [[Gen.4.26|Genesis 4:26]], almost the first mention of prayer in the Bible.
A humble, earnest request; a prayer.
Elijah. The King James New Testament uses the Greek form of his name. He prayed on Mount Carmel, first for fire and then for rain ([[1Kgs.18.42|1 Kings 18:42]]).
A small child’s first, unclear words.
A song or prayer for the dead; here, a dying believer’s last song.
From [[Song.2.4|Song of Solomon 2:4]], “He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.”

modern:
Everything on earth needs to be renewed. Nothing God made keeps going by itself. “Thou renewest the face of the year,” said the psalmist. Even trees, which don’t wear themselves out with worry or shorten their lives with hard work, have to drink the rain from the sky and draw up the hidden riches of the soil. The cedars of Lebanon, which God planted, stay alive only because every day they fill with fresh sap drawn up from the earth.

Human life can’t be kept going without God renewing it either. Just as the body needs regular meals to make up for what it uses, the soul needs feeding too: on the Bible, on the preaching of the Word, and at the rich table of the church’s ordinances. How low our graces sink when we neglect the ways God feeds us! What starved little things some Christians are, living without careful use of God’s Word and private prayer! If our faith can live without God, God didn’t make it. It’s only a dream. If God had given it life, it would wait on him the way flowers wait for the dew.

Without constant renewal we aren’t ready for hell’s endless attacks, or the hard trials heaven sends, or even the battles going on inside us. When the whirlwind is let loose, it’s bad news for the tree that hasn’t drawn up fresh sap and gripped the rock with deep, tangled roots. When storms come, it’s bad news for the sailors who haven’t strengthened their mast, dropped their anchor or made for the harbor. If we let the good in us grow weaker, the evil will surely grow stronger and fight hard to take control of us. Then painful ruin and shameful disgrace may follow. So let’s come humbly before God’s mercy and ask, and we’ll see the promise come true: “They that wait on the Lord shall renew their strength.”

notes.note: Continues, keeps going. The old -eth ending is today’s -s.

notes.term: “Thou renewest the face of the year”
notes.note: Spurgeon is quoting from memory. [[Ps.104.30|Psalm 104:30]] reads “thou renewest the face of the earth.”
The means of grace: the ordinary ways God feeds faith, such as the Bible, prayer, preaching and the Lord’s Supper.
The practices Christ gave the church, chiefly baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Spurgeon calls them a “soul-fattening table” because they nourish faith.
Thin, underfed creatures.
Devotion to God; faith as it’s actually lived.
An old warning: “how terrible it will be for…”
The place at a king’s feet where someone kneels to ask a favor; here, coming to God in prayer.
[[Isa.40.31|Isaiah 40:31]]. The King James wording is “wait upon the Lord.”

modern:
Jesus Christ himself is the whole sum and substance of the covenant, and as one of its gifts he belongs to every believer. Believer, can you begin to measure what you have in Christ? “In him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.” Think about that word “God” and everything infinite in it, and then think about “perfect man” and all his beauty. Everything Christ ever had or ever can have, as God and as man, is yours. It has been handed over to you out of pure, free kindness, to be yours forever, an inheritance that can never be taken away.

As God, our blessed Jesus knows everything, is present everywhere and can do anything. Isn’t it a comfort to know that all these great and glorious qualities are completely yours? Does he have power? That power is yours, to hold you up and make you strong, to defeat your enemies and keep you safe right to the end. Does he have love? There isn’t one drop of love in his heart that isn’t yours. You can dive into the endless ocean of his love and say of all of it, “It is mine.” Does he have justice? That may sound like a stern quality, but even that is yours, because his justice will make sure that everything promised to you in the covenant of grace is given to you without fail.

And everything he has as *perfect man* is yours too. As a perfect man, he had his Father’s delight resting on him. The Most High accepted him. Believer, God’s acceptance of Christ is your acceptance. Don’t you know that the love the Father set on a perfect Christ, he sets on you *now*? Everything Christ did is yours. The perfect righteousness Jesus worked out when he kept the law through his spotless life, and showed how honorable it is, is yours. It is counted as yours. Christ is in the covenant.

notes.note: God’s binding promise to save his people through Christ, freely, as a gift and not a reward. This is the “covenant of grace,” and the day’s text says God gives Christ himself as part of it.

notes.term: “In him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily”
notes.note: [[Col.2.9|Colossians 2:9]]: everything God is lives in Christ, in a human body.
An old legal term for an estate fixed to pass down a family line, which could never be sold off or taken away.
All-knowing, present everywhere, all-powerful.
From [[Isa.42.21|Isaiah 42:21]], “he will magnify the law, and make it honourable.” By keeping God’s law perfectly, Jesus showed how good it is.
Credited to someone’s account. Christ’s righteousness is counted as the believer’s own, as if they had lived his perfect life.
The opening of a hymn by Charles Wesley.

modern: The voice crying in the wilderness called for *a way for the Lord, a way made ready, and a way made ready in the wilderness*. I want to listen to the Master’s announcement and give him a road into my heart, built up by the work of his grace across the desert of my nature. The four instructions in this text deserve my serious attention.

*Every valley must be lifted up.* Low, groveling thoughts of God have to go. Doubt and despair have to be cleared away. Selfishness and the pleasures of the flesh have to be left behind. A glorious raised road of grace must be built across these deep valleys.

*Every mountain and hill shall be laid low.* Proud self-sufficiency and boastful self-righteousness must be leveled to make a highway for the King of kings. God never grants close fellowship with himself to proud, arrogant sinners. The Lord pays attention to the humble and visits those whose hearts are broken over sin, but he detests the proud. My soul, beg the Holy Spirit to put you right in this.

*The crooked shall be made straight.* A wavering heart needs a straight path marked out for it: a firm decision for God and holiness. Double-minded people are strangers to the God of truth. My soul, take care to be honest and true in everything, as someone living in the sight of the God who searches hearts.

*The rough places shall be made smooth.* The stumbling blocks of sin must be cleared away, and the thorns and briers of rebellion pulled up by the roots. When so great a visitor comes to honor his favored ones with his company, he mustn’t find muddy tracks and stony ground. Oh, that this evening the Lord would find a highway in my heart, made ready by his grace, so that he can travel in triumph through every corner of my soul, from the beginning of this year right to the end of it.

notes.term: The voice crying in the wilderness
notes.note: John the Baptist, getting people ready for Jesus. He was quoting [[Isa.40.3-Isa.40.4|Isaiah 40:3–4]], and Spurgeon’s four “directions” follow Isaiah’s wording.
Built up, the way a raised road is piled up across low ground ([[Isa.62.10|Isaiah 62:10]], “cast up the highway”).
Raised up, lifted high.
Of the flesh: the desires of our fallen human nature, not only sexual ones.
A created being thinking it has all it needs in itself, without God.
Graciously given or granted.
From [[Ps.138.6|Psalm 138:6]], “yet hath he respect unto the lowly: but the proud he knoweth afar off.”
Crushed with sorrow over sin.
Pulled two ways, unable to commit. “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways” ([[Jas.1.8|James 1:8]]).
Muddy, boggy.

modern:
“Grow in grace”—not just in one grace, but in *all* of them. Grow in *faith*, the root every other grace grows from. Believe the promises more firmly than you have before. Let your faith grow fuller, steadier and simpler. Grow in *love* too. Ask that your love would reach further, run deeper and show itself more in practice, shaping every thought, word and action. Grow in *humility* as well. Aim to be very low in your own eyes, and to see more and more how small you are. And as you grow *downward* in humility, seek to grow *upward* too, coming nearer to God in prayer and into closer friendship with Jesus.

May God the Holy Spirit help you to “*grow in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour*.” Anyone who doesn’t grow in knowing Jesus is turning a blessing away. To know him is “life eternal,” and to go further in knowing him is to grow in happiness. If you don’t long to know more of Christ, you don’t know him at all yet. Anyone who has had a sip of this wine will be thirsty for more. Christ does satisfy, but it’s the kind of satisfaction that doesn’t dull your appetite. It sharpens it. If you know the love of Jesus, you’ll long for deeper drinks of his love, the way a deer pants for streams of water. If you don’t want to know him better, then you don’t love him, because love always cries, “Nearer, nearer.”

To be away from Christ is hell, but to be with Jesus is heaven. So don’t settle down until you’re getting to know Jesus better and better. Seek to know more of him: in his nature as God, in his life as a man, in his finished work, in his death, in his resurrection, in the glorious way he prays for us now, and in his coming again as King. Stay close beside the cross, and search out the mystery of his wounds. Loving Jesus more, and understanding more fully how he loves us, is one of the best signs that we’re growing in grace.

notes.note: Spurgeon pictures faith as the root that the other graces, such as love, humility and hope, grow from.
From [[John.17.3|John 17:3]], “this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ.”
“Cloyed” means sickened by too much of something sweet. “Whetted” means sharpened, like a blade on a stone.
From [[Ps.42.1|Psalm 42:1]], “As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.” A hart is a male deer.
Drinks; long swallows.
Praying for someone else. Jesus now “ever liveth to make intercession” for his people ([[Heb.7.25|Hebrews 7:25]]).
A coming or arrival. His “royal advent” is his return as King.
Stay close beside. “Hard by” is old English for “right next to.”
Grasp or understanding, not worry.

modern: This morning we longed to grow in knowing the Lord Jesus. Tonight it may be good to think about a related subject: *our heavenly Joseph’s knowledge of us*. His knowledge of us was perfect, wonderfully so, long before we knew the first thing about him. “His eyes beheld our substance, yet being imperfect, and in his book all our members were written, when as yet there was none of them.” Before we existed in the world, we existed in his heart. When we were his enemies, he knew us: our misery, our madness and our wickedness. When we wept bitterly in hopeless repentance and saw him only as a judge and ruler, he saw us as his dearly loved brothers, and his heart ached with love for us. He never mistook his chosen ones. He always saw them as the objects of his endless love. “The Lord knoweth them that are his” is as true of the prodigals still feeding pigs as it is of the children sitting at the table.

But sadly, *we didn’t know our royal Brother*, and a whole crowd of sins grew out of that ignorance. We kept our hearts from him and wouldn’t let him into our love. We didn’t trust him or believe what he said. We rebelled against him and gave him no loving honor. The Sun of Righteousness shone out, and we couldn’t see him. Heaven came down to earth, and earth didn’t notice. Praise God, those days are over for us. Yet even now we know very little of Jesus compared with how much he knows of us. We’ve only just begun to study him, but he knows us completely. It’s a blessing that the ignorance isn’t on his side, because if it were, our case would be hopeless. He won’t say to us, “I never knew you.” He’ll own our names openly on the day he appears, and until then he’ll show himself to us in a way he doesn’t show himself to the world.

notes.note: When Joseph’s brothers came to Egypt for food, he recognized them but they didn’t recognize him ([[Gen.42.8|Genesis 42:8]]). Spurgeon sees Jesus the same way: he knows us long before we know him.
Spurgeon reworks [[Ps.139.16|Psalm 139:16]]. “Substance” is the body as it was being formed in the womb; “members” are its parts.
His deepest feelings were stirred. The King James Bible places tender feelings in the gut, the way we place them in the heart. It’s said of Joseph in [[Gen.43.30|Genesis 43:30]].

notes.term: “The Lord knoweth them that are his”

notes.note: People who waste everything, from Jesus’ story of the son who spent his inheritance and ended up feeding pigs ([[Luke.15.15|Luke 15:15]]).
A name for Christ from [[Mal.4.2|Malachi 4:2]].
What Jesus will say to those who only claimed to follow him ([[Matt.7.23|Matthew 7:23]]).
Openly acknowledge us as his own ([[Rev.3.5|Revelation 3:5]]).
Show himself. From [[John.14.22|John 14:22]], “how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?”

modern: No wonder light is good, since it came from that good command, “Let there be light.” We who enjoy light should be more thankful for it than we are, and see more of God in it and by it. Solomon says *physical* light is sweet, but *gospel* light is far more precious, because it shows us eternal things and feeds the part of us that will never die. When the Holy Spirit gives us *spiritual* light, and opens our eyes to see the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, we see sin in its true colors and ourselves as we really are. We see the Most Holy God as he shows himself, his plan of mercy as he sets it out, and the world to come as his Word describes it. Spiritual light has many beams and many colors, like light through a prism, but whether they’re knowledge, joy, holiness or life, they’re all good, because they all come from God. If the light we receive is this good, what must Light itself be, the *very source* of light? And how glorious must the place be where he shows himself? O Lord, since light is so good, give us more of it, and more of yourself, the true light.

As soon as there’s anything good in the world, *a dividing line is needed*. Light and darkness have nothing in common. God has separated them, so let’s not mix them up. Children of light mustn’t have anything to do with the deeds, teachings or deceptions of darkness. Children of the day must be clear-headed, honest and bold in their Lord’s work, and leave the works of darkness to those who will live in darkness forever. Our churches should separate the light from the darkness by church discipline, and we should do the same by living clearly apart from the world. In what we judge, what we do, what we listen to, what we teach and who we join with, we must tell the precious from the worthless, and keep the great distinction the Lord made on the world’s first day. O Lord Jesus, be our light all through this day, for your light is the light of men.

notes.note: A command that makes something happen; Latin for “let it be done.”

notes.term: Said by Solomon to be sweet
notes.note: [[Eccl.11.7|Ecclesiastes 11:7]], “Truly the light is sweet.”

notes.term: The glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ
notes.note: From [[2Cor.4.6|2 Corinthians 4:6]].
Puts forward, sets out.
The rainbow of colors that appears when light passes through a prism.
Light in its very essence: God himself, who “is light” ([[1John.1.5|1 John 1:5]]).
Nothing shared. It echoes [[2Cor.6.14|2 Corinthians 6:14]], “what communion hath light with darkness?”
Confuse, mix up.
Clear-headed and self-controlled, not only “not drunk” ([[1Thess.5.5-1Thess.5.8|1 Thessalonians 5:5–8]]).
From [[Jer.15.19|Jeremiah 15:19]]. “Vile” here means worthless.

modern:
This morning we noticed how good light is, and how the Lord divided it from the darkness. Now we notice the special way the Lord looked at the light. “God saw the light”—he looked at it with satisfaction, gazed at it with pleasure, and saw that it “was good.” Dear reader, if the Lord has given you light, he looks at that light with a very special interest. It’s precious to him not only because he made it, but because it’s like him, for “He is light.”

It’s a lovely thing for a believer to know that God’s eye watches so tenderly over the work of grace he has begun. He never loses sight of the treasure he has put in our clay jars. Sometimes we can’t see the light, but God always sees it, and that’s far better than our seeing it. Better for the judge to see that I’m innocent than for me to think I can see it. It’s very comforting to know that I’m one of God’s people. But whether *I* know it or not, if the Lord knows it, I’m still safe. This is the foundation: “The Lord knoweth them that are his.”

You may be sighing and groaning over the sin that still lives in you, and grieving over your darkness, yet the Lord sees “light” in your heart, because he put it there. All the clouds and gloom in your soul can’t hide your light from his kind eye. You may have sunk deep into discouragement, even despair. But if your soul has any longing toward Christ, and if you’re trying to rest in his finished work, God sees the “light.” He doesn’t only *see* it; he also *keeps* it alive in you. “I, the Lord, do keep it.” That’s a precious thought for anyone who has anxiously watched over themselves and found they can’t keep themselves at all. The light he keeps by his grace, he will one day bring to the full blaze of noon and the fullness of glory. The light inside you is the dawn of the day that never ends.

notes.note: In Spurgeon’s day, quiet pleasure and satisfaction, without today’s sense of being smug.
[[1John.1.5|1 John 1:5]], “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.”
Clay jars. “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” ([[2Cor.4.7|2 Corinthians 4:7]]): God’s great gift kept in ordinary, breakable people.

notes.term: “The Lord knoweth them that are his”

notes.note: The sinful nature we’re born with, which still lives in believers.
Feeling low and discouraged.
Everything Jesus did to save us, completed on the cross. “It is finished” ([[John.19.30|John 19:30]]).
[[Isa.27.3|Isaiah 27:3]], God speaking of his vineyard, his people.

modern: It’s a happy way to calm our sorrow when we can feel, “HE careth for me.” Christian, don’t dishonor your faith by always going around with a worried frown. Come, throw your burden onto your Lord. You’re staggering under a weight your Father wouldn’t even feel. What seems a crushing load to you is to him no more than a speck of dust on the scales. Nothing is as sweet as to

Suffering child of God, be patient. God hasn’t overlooked you in his care. He feeds the sparrows, and he’ll give you what you need as well. Don’t sit down in despair. Keep hoping, and never stop. Take up the weapons of faith against a sea of trouble, and by fighting back you’ll yet bring your troubles to an end. *There is* One who cares for you. His eye is on you, his heart beats with pity for your pain, and his all-powerful hand will still bring you the help you need. The darkest cloud will break up in showers of mercy. The blackest gloom will give way to morning. If you’re one of his family, he’ll bandage your wounds and heal your broken heart. Don’t doubt his grace because you’re in trouble. Believe that he loves you as much in hard times as in happy ones.

What a calm, peaceful life you could lead if you’d leave the providing to the God who provides! With a little oil in the jar and a handful of flour in the barrel, Elijah outlasted the famine, and so will you. If God cares for you, why do you need to worry as well? Can you trust him with your soul and not with your body? He has never refused to carry your burdens, and he has never collapsed under their weight. So come, dear soul, be done with fretful worry, and leave everything that concerns you in the hands of a gracious God.

notes.note: Spurgeon turns the day’s text ([[1Pet.5.7|1 Peter 5:7]]) into the believer’s own words. “Careth” means “cares.”

notes.term: The small dust of the balance
notes.note: A speck of dust on a pair of weighing scales, too light to tip them. [[Isa.40.15|Isaiah 40:15]] says the nations are like this to God.
Lie still and yield, not struggling against God’s will.
God’s care and control over everything that happens, providing for his people. “The God of providence” is the God who provides.
Jesus said our heavenly Father feeds the birds, and we matter far more to him ([[Matt.6.26|Matthew 6:26]]).

notes.term: Arms of faith against a sea of trouble
notes.note: A nod to Hamlet’s “to take arms against a sea of troubles, and by opposing end them.”
A small jar. In a famine, God kept a widow’s little oil and flour from running out while Elijah stayed with her ([[1Kgs.17.12-1Kgs.17.16|1 Kings 17:12–16]]).
From [[Ps.147.3|Psalm 147:3]], “He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.”
Anxious and restless with worry.

modern:
This may come as *judgment*. If so, let me think about why such a visit has come, and accept the rod and the One who sent it. I’m not the only one who is disciplined in the night. Let me submit to the trouble cheerfully and work hard to gain something from it.

But the hand of the Lord can also be felt in another way: strengthening the soul and lifting the spirit up toward eternal things. Oh, that I may feel the Lord dealing with me like this! A sense that God is present, and living within us, carries the soul up toward heaven as if on eagles’ wings. At times like that we’re full to the brim with spiritual joy and forget the worries and sorrows of earth. The unseen is near, and the seen loses its hold on us. The body, like a servant, waits at the foot of the hill, while the spirit, its master, worships at the top in the presence of the Lord. Oh, that God would grant me a holy time of close fellowship with him this evening! The Lord knows I need it badly. My graces are wilting, my sinful desires are raging, my faith is weak, my devotion is cold. All these are reasons why he should lay his healing hand on me.

His hand can cool my burning forehead and quiet my pounding heart. That glorious right hand that shaped the world can make my mind new. The tireless hand that holds up the earth’s huge pillars can hold up my spirit. The loving hand that holds all the saints can hold me close. And the mighty hand that smashes the enemy can conquer my sins. Why shouldn’t I feel that hand touching me this evening? Come, my soul, speak to your God with this powerful plea: Jesus’ hands were pierced to set you free. Then you’ll surely feel that same hand on you, the hand that once touched Daniel and set him on his knees so that he could see visions of God.

notes.term: The hand of the Lord was upon me
notes.note: In Ezekiel this means God came on him with power, often before a vision or a message.

modern:
Believers haven’t always lived for Christ. A person starts to when God the Holy Spirit convicts them of sin, and when by grace they’re brought to see the dying Savior paying for their guilt. From the moment of that new birth from heaven, they begin to live for Christ. To believers, Jesus is the one pearl of great price, and we’d give up everything we have for him. He has won our love so completely that our hearts beat for him alone. We’d live for his glory and die defending his gospel. He’s the pattern for our lives, the model we want to shape our character on.

Paul’s words mean more than most people think. They mean the *whole aim and purpose of his life* was Christ. More than that, his life itself was Jesus. As an old saint put it, he ate and drank and slept eternal life. Jesus was his very breath, the soul of his soul, the heart of his heart, the life of his life.

As someone who says you’re a Christian, can you say you live up to this? Can you honestly say that for you to live is Christ? Your work: are you doing it *for Christ*? Or is it done to get ahead and to benefit your family? Do you ask, “Is that a mean reason?” For a *Christian*, it is. Christians say they live for Christ, so how can they live for something else without being spiritually unfaithful to him? Plenty of people live by this principle to some extent, but who would dare to say they have lived wholly for Christ, the way the apostle did? Yet this alone is the true life of a Christian: its source, what keeps it going, its shape and its goal, all gathered up in one word, Christ Jesus.

Lord, accept me. I offer myself to you here, praying to live only in you and for you. Let me be like the ox that stands between the plow and the altar, ready to work or to be sacrificed, and let my motto be, “Ready for either.”

notes.note: A sacrifice that turns God’s anger away by fully paying for sin ([[1John.2.2|1 John 2:2]]).
From Jesus’ parable of the merchant who sold everything he had to buy one priceless pearl ([[Matt.13.45-Matt.13.46|Matthew 13:45–46]]).
Someone who claims, or “professes,” to be a Christian.
Making yourself bigger, richer or more important.
Here, low or unworthy, not unkind.
The Bible’s picture of loving something else in God’s place as unfaithfulness in a marriage ([[Jas.4.4|James 4:4]]).

notes.term: The bullock between the plough and the altar
notes.note: An old emblem of a willing servant: an ox standing between a plow (work) and an altar (sacrifice), under the motto “Ready for either.”

modern:
Notice the sweet names the heavenly Solomon uses, with deep affection, for his bride, the church. “*My sister*: someone close to me by family ties, who shares my feelings. *My spouse*: nearest and dearest, joined to me by the tenderest bonds of love, my sweet companion, part of my own self. *My sister*, because I became human, which makes me bone of your bone and flesh of your flesh. *My spouse*, because of our engagement in heaven, where I promised myself to you in righteousness. *My sister*, whom I knew long ago and watched over from her earliest childhood. *My spouse*, chosen from among the daughters, held in arms of love and promised to me forever.”

See how true it is that our royal Kinsman, the King who is also our family, isn’t ashamed of us. He dwells with obvious delight on this double relationship. Our King James Bible has the word “my” twice, as if Christ lingered with joy on the fact that the church is his. “His delights were with the sons of men,” because those sons of men were his own chosen ones. He, the Shepherd, went looking for the sheep because they were *his* sheep. He came “to seek and to save that which was lost,” because what was lost was *his* long before it was lost to itself or lost to him. The church belongs to her Lord alone. No one else may claim a share in her or pretend to a part of her love. Jesus, your church is glad to have it so!

Let every believing soul drink comfort from these wells. Dear soul, Christ is close to you by family ties. Christ is dear to you by the bond of marriage, and you are dear to him. Look, he takes both your hands in both of his and says, “*My* sister, *my* spouse.” See the two holy grips by which your Lord holds you twice over, so that he can’t and won’t ever let you go. Dear friend, don’t be slow to return the holy flame of his love.

notes.note: Christ. Spurgeon reads the Song of Solomon as a picture of Christ’s love for his church.

notes.term: Bone of thy bone and flesh of thy flesh
notes.note: Adam’s words about Eve ([[Gen.2.23|Genesis 2:23]]). By becoming human, Christ shares our nature.
